title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
summary: You get a list `nums` of integers. It was sorted from smallest to largest and then rotated: split into two pieces that swapped places, so it may now start partway through the sorted order. The rotation may also have left it unchanged. Return the smallest number in `nums`. Your search must run in O(log n) time, where n is the length of `nums`.

examples.explanation: This is [3, 8, 11, 15, 22, 27] rotated so that it starts at 15.
The rotation left the list in sorted order, so the smallest number comes first.

constraints: No value appears twice in nums

approaches.twist: Compare the middle value with the last one in the range: if it's larger, the minimum lies right of mid; if not, it's at mid or to its left.
Scan every number and keep the smallest one you've seen.
approaches.note: Works, but it reads every number: O(n) time. The target is O(log n).

signals.meaning: A rotated sorted list is two sorted runs, and the smallest number starts the second one. Comparing the middle with the end of the range tells you which run mid is in.
Both pieces are still sorted, and every number in the first piece is larger than every number in the second, so one comparison places mid.
Scanning for the minimum is O(n). To reach log n, each step has to rule out half of the range.

constraintReading: len(nums) is at most 5000, so a scan would be quick: the O(log n) requirement is what rules out O(n). Halving 5000 numbers takes about 13 steps, and lo and hi need only O(1) extra space.

hints.clarify: What does a rotated list look like? Two sorted runs, where every number of the first run is bigger than every number of the second: [7, 9, 1, 3, 5] is [1, 3, 5, 7, 9] rotated. The smallest number starts the second run. If the list wasn't rotated at all, there's only one run, and the smallest number comes first.
hints.approach: Binary search, comparing the middle with the last number of the range. If `nums[mid]` is bigger than `nums[hi]`, mid is in the first run, so the minimum lies to the right of mid: `lo` = mid + 1. Otherwise mid is in the second run (or the list is sorted from mid to hi), so the minimum is mid itself or to its left: `hi` = mid. When `lo` meets `hi`, it sits on the minimum.
hints.whyNot: Scanning for the smallest number is O(n). Comparing the middle with the first number of the range is trickier: on a list that wasn't rotated, `nums[mid]` is bigger than `nums[lo]` and yet the minimum is on the left, so you'd need a special case. The last number never misleads: the minimum's run always ends the range.

slots.setup: `lo` = 0 and `hi` = the last index: the minimum is somewhere in between.
slots.loop: Keep going while `lo` < `hi`; when they meet, one candidate is left, and it's the minimum.
slots.update: If `nums[mid]` > `nums[hi]`, set `lo` = mid + 1; otherwise set `hi` = mid, not mid − 1, because mid itself may be the minimum.
slots.record: Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]` to tell which run mid is in.

solution.explanation: Each step halves the range from `lo` to `hi`, so the loop runs about log₂ n times: O(log n) time. Only `lo`, `hi` and `mid` are stored: O(1) space. The minimum always stays inside the range: `lo` only skips numbers of the first run, which are all bigger than the minimum, and `hi` = mid keeps mid in play.

events.label: compare
events.say: The middle of nums[{lo}..{hi}] is nums[{mid}] = {nums[mid]}. Compare it with the last number of the range, nums[{hi}] = {nums[hi]}

events.label: go right
events.say: {nums[mid]} is bigger than {nums[hi]}, so mid is in the first, higher run: the minimum is to the right of mid

events.label: go left
events.say: {nums[mid]} is not bigger than {nums[hi]}, so mid to hi is sorted: the minimum is mid itself or to its left

events.label: return
events.say: lo and hi met at index {lo}, so the minimum is {nums[lo]}

predict.ask: Is the minimum to the right of mid?
Is the minimum to the right of mid?

related.relation: Halves the list the same way, but there's no target: the middle is compared with the end of the range instead.
The same rotated list, but you look for a given value, so at each step you work out which half is sorted and whether the target lies in it.
